There is plenty of GOP hand-wringing about the Senate, for good reason. According to polling averages from Real Clear Politics, Democrats are leading in nine of 11 close Senate races (Republicans are leading in Florida and—narrowly—in Kansas). If Democrats win those races, that’s it. They will control the Senate.

   But, slow down. Let’s look under the hood.

   The leads are SLIM   Aside from Georgia and New Hampshire, the Democratic leads are 3 percentage points or less. That means, when factoring in a “margin of error,” anything could be possible. So if these polling averages skew toward Democrats, and Election Day turns out stronger than expected for Republicans, well, there ya go.

   Trump overperformed in the Senate in 2018   Everyone remembers Nancy Pelosi taking the gavel after the 2018 midterms when Democrats picked up 41 House seats. In that same midterm, Republicans picked up two Senate seats, widening their majority in the upper chamber. Midterms can yield strange results, and if voters end up balking at Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, and then Republicans hold off Democrats in other close races, it could happen again.

   Democrats need low-propensity voters   To win many of these Senate seats, Democrats are going to likely need young independent voters who typically shy away from elections (President Trump did a great job of overperforming with this group in 2024). Relying on unreliable voters is, well, fraught. This is also a group of voters who tend to think politics is rife with corruption and that both parties are to blame. That’s a heck of a gamble by Democrats. If they don’t turn out in droves, advantage to the GOP.

The Case for Republicans to Hold the Senate
 
Plus, seven candidates tell The Journal how they would fix Congress, and an Abdul El-Sayed opponent handed him a viral campaign highlight
 
 
BLAKE FAGAN/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. There is plenty of GOP hand-wringing about the Senate, for good reason. According to polling averages from Real Clear Politics, Democrats are leading in nine of 11 close Senate races (Republicans are leading in Florida and—narrowly—in Kansas). If Democrats win those races, that’s it. They will control the Senate.

 

But, slow down. Let’s look under the hood.

 

The leads are SLIM

 

Aside from Georgia and New Hampshire, the Democratic leads are 3 percentage points or less. That means, when factoring in a “margin of error,” anything could be possible. So if these polling averages skew toward Democrats, and Election Day turns out stronger than expected for Republicans, well, there ya go.

 

Trump overperformed in the Senate in 2018

 

Everyone remembers Nancy Pelosi taking the gavel after the 2018 midterms when Democrats picked up 41 House seats. Midterms can yield strange results, and if voters end up balking at Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, and then Republicans hold off Democrats in other close races, it could happen again.

 

Democrats need low-propensity voters

 

To win many of these Senate seats, Democrats are going to likely need young independent voters who typically shy away from elections (President Trump did a great job of overperforming with this group in 2024). Relying on unreliable voters is, well, fraught. This is also a group of voters who tend to think politics is rife with corruption and that both parties are to blame. That’s a heck of a gamble by Democrats. If they don’t turn out in droves, advantage to the GOP.

Congress is broken. Here’s how seven candidates would fix it. The up-and-coming congressional candidates who sat down with The Wall Street Journal before the midterm elections all agreed on one point: Things need to change on Capitol Hill. We asked them how to fix the most pressing problems facing Congress. This is what they said.
